No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon. The Pentagon has acknowledged U.S. casualties in the war with Iran are higher than previously announced, now standing at 22. NPR's Quill Lawrence reports.
A Pentagon spokesman told NPR the way casualties are being counted is being standardized and that the department will begin posting numbers that are "pending adjudication" and may change.
But this is not the first time the Trump administration has abruptly posted new numbers or changed the way it counts casualties from the Iran war, spreading the numbers of wounded in action, killed in action, and non-combat casualties as if they were not part of the same war.
Two leading Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee said in a statement that while they were glad to see the error had been corrected, there is "no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude."
Quill Lawrence, NPR News. President Trump signed an executive order this week designed to help lower diesel costs for farmers, at least temporarily.
South Dakota Public Broadcasting's Jackson Dirks reports.
Larry Bergen is loading soybeans into a truck. Trump's order lets farmers use dyed diesel in trucks like this until the end of the year.
It's exempt from federal taxes and normally reserved for off-road machinery. Bergen says it helps during harvest season.
We've got a long ways to go as far as how many times I'm going to fill. So it makes a lot of difference, yes.
It saves farmers about 24 cents a gallon in taxes, but diesel is still about 60 percent more expensive than this time last year. Scott Vanderwall is president of South Dakota's Farm Bureau.
It's a little bit of a band-aid. It certainly doesn't make up the difference.
Farmers helped Trump get into office. More than 60 percent of the vote in agriculture-heavy South Dakota went to Trump the last three elections.
For NPR News, I'm Jackson Dirks in Beersford, South Dakota.
A new report in The Lancet says obesity is projected to become one of the largest threats to human health by the end of the century.
As NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports, that's just one of 17 threats to global health.
Rather than focusing on a single threat, the report brought together global data on how over a dozen risk factors influence health.
Those factors are varied, including air pollution, high blood pressure, and declining foreign aid.
The team estimated the number of years in good health that could be lost because of each factor over the next 75 years.
Over 23 billion years could be lost to obesity, making it the biggest single threat.
Income inequality and low educational attainment were the next biggest threats to health, though both have substantial uncertainty.
To combat all these threats, the report recommends bolstering health system readiness, investing in new technologies, and beefing up health surveillance.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
At least four people died after the first hurricane of the Atlantic season swept across the Florida panhandle and then into Alabama.
Hundreds of thousands lost power. You're listening to NPR.
Nine people, including children, are dead after a massive shooting last night in Erie, Pennsylvania.
NPR's Chantalice Duster has more.
Erie police say a woman who was eight months pregnant and a 10-month-old baby were among those killed in the shooting that took place at her home.
The suspected gunman also died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to police.
Police responded to an alert of gunshots at the home, and when they arrived, they found two women dead outside.
Investigators believe the deaths occurred before law enforcement arrived.
Eight people were family members, and one was a family friend, according to police.
Erie police say they are investigating a possible motive.
They also said the suspected shooter had a history with law enforcement but did not give details.
Chantalice Duster, NPR News.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has refused to comment on a report that the U.S. Ambassador to Greece engaged in improper and possibly illegal activity in the days before her confirmation hearing.
Secretary Rubio was asked to comment while on his way to Greece.
The story, published in the Wall Street Journal, said Kimberly Guilfoyle asked a campaign donor and supporter of President Trump to pay for her $100,000 credit card bill.
The report says in return, Guilfoyle promised the donor he would have access to high-level administrations, including the president.
Vice President J.D. Vance was also asked about the report.
He said, "If there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer the consequences for it."
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
